paragraphs.text: Loose leaf from Yunnan, made as [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) and then left unpressed to age. Its leaf went through the [wet pile](shou:wet-piling): it was wetted and heaped so that heat, moisture and microbes could work on it, then dried. Yunnan’s state factories brought that method into production in 1973.
Ripe pu’er is ready to drink soon after it is made, unlike raw pu’er, which usually waits years. The time this leaf has spent aging loose goes beyond what its making required.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water and forgives a heavy hand. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml, one quick rinse, then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
